content: This structure is analogous to the mandible, which is similarly formed by the fusion of two halves at the mental symphysis. The alveolar process of the maxilla is responsible for holding the upper teeth and is commonly referred to as the maxillary arch. The maxilla connects laterally to the zygomatic bones, which are also known as the cheekbones. Additionally, the maxilla plays a critical role in forming the boundaries of three anatomical cavities: the roof of the mouth, the floor and lateral wall of the nasal cavity (or nasal antrum), and the floor of the orbit. Each half of the maxilla, which is fused at the midline, is composed of the body of the maxilla and four distinct processes. These processes include the zygomatic process, the frontal process, the alveolar process, and the palatine process. Additionally, the infraorbital foramen is a notable feature of the maxilla. The maxilla articulates with a total of nine bones. These include two bones of the cranium, specifically the frontal bone and the ethmoid bone, as well as seven bones of the face. The facial bones that articulate with the maxilla are the nasal bone, the zygomatic bone, the lacrimal bone, the inferior nasal concha, the palatine bone, the vomer, and the adjacent fused maxillary bone. In some cases, the maxilla may also articulate with the orbital surface or the lateral pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone. Additional anatomical images of the maxilla illustrate its relationships and articulations. These include depictions of the seven bones that form the orbit, the facial bones, the outer surface of the left maxilla, the nasal surface of the left maxilla, the left maxillary sinus as viewed from the exterior, the bony palate and alveolar arch, the sphenoid bone (visible in the center-right region), the articulation of the left palatine bone with the maxilla, and a side view of the teeth and jaws.
